summary: BBN's report on host availability from September 30 to October 8, 1971, with a table of daily test logins. It also notes that three more hosts could now act as servers. It was replaced by RFC 255.

eli5.summary: A report card showing which network computers answered the phone on which days, with a note that a few more can now accept visitors.

subtitle: ARPANET host status report for October 1971, noting new servers.

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators and administrators needed regular updates on which hosts were functioning and could act as network servers.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested each host daily and published biweekly status reports with host availability tables and predictions from site operators.
tldr.outcome: Three more hosts—SRI NIC, MIT Multics, and Harvard—became able to serve the network, expanding available services.

facts.label: Status codes
facts.value: 5 (Open, Dead, Timed out, Half Open, Refused)

today: RFC 252 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 255. It documents the early growth of ARPANET server capacity in fall 1971.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 252 reports on ARPANET host status from September 30 through October 8, 1971. It notes that during September 27-29 the BBN Terminal IMP was offline for hardware debugging and therefore not available to test hosts. Three hosts that were not official servers in RFC 240 had since become able to act as servers: SRI's PDP-10, MIT Multics, and Harvard's PDP-10, though Harvard had limited core memory and would run Telnet only occasionally.
sections.eli5: A report from the first week of October showed that a few more computers could now accept visitors, though Harvard's would only accept them once in a while.

sections.title: Daily Test Results and Status Codes
sections.content: Testing continued with the same methodology from RFC 240. The report includes a table of daily results for hosts from September 30 to October 8. Several status codes indicated host connectivity: O meant open and accessible, D meant dead or unreachable, T meant timed out, H meant half-open, and R meant refused. Some sites advertised unavailable times. The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered only Remote Job Service and did not yet have a full Telnet server.
sections.eli5: Each day showed which computers answered and which did not, using the same letter codes as before to show what happened each call.

sections.title: Host Predictions and Server Status
sections.content: The report includes a table of 15 hosts with their predicted status, obtained from operators at each site. Most were expected to become servers; some remained user-only (the Terminal IMPs). Several hosts showed unstable behavior, such as Lincoln's IBM-360 (frequently half-open or dead) and SDC's IBM-360 (always dead during this period, though the report did not explain why).
sections.eli5: Each host's operator said whether their computer would be available as a shared service, and the results showed which promises came true.
